tool.name: Zsh
tool.tagline: Interactive shell with powerful completion, globbing and customization
tool.description: Zsh is a Bourne-style Unix shell, largely compatible with bash, that adds a programmable completion system, rich globbing, a highly configurable line editor and prompt, and a large plugin ecosystem. It has been the default shell on macOS since Catalina, and many developers on Linux adopt it for a faster, friendlier terminal. Learning it well means fewer keystrokes every day and a shell configuration you understand rather than copy-paste.

concepts.name: Zsh vs bash, and switching
concepts.summary: What zsh adds over bash, how to check which shell you are in and how to make zsh your login shell.
concepts.why: You need to know which shell is reading your commands before any configuration makes sense.
concepts.body:
Zsh is a Bourne-family shell, so everyday command lines, pipes, redirections, variables, `if` and `for` work as in bash. What it adds is mostly for interactive use: a far smarter completion system, recursive globbing with filters, spelling correction, shared history, a programmable line editor and prompt, and a big plugin ecosystem. It has been the default login shell on **macOS since 10.15 Catalina**; on Linux you install it with your package manager.

Two variables are easy to confuse. `$SHELL` is your **login shell** as recorded in the user database, not necessarily the shell you are running right now; `ps -p $$` or `echo $ZSH_VERSION` tells you the current one. Change your login shell with `chsh -s "$(command -v zsh)"`; the path must be listed in `/etc/shells`, and the change applies at your next login.

The first time zsh starts without a `~/.zshrc` it offers the `zsh-newuser-install` menu; you can quit it and write the file yourself. `zsh -f` starts a shell with **no** startup files, handy for testing whether a problem comes from your config.

Switching your interactive shell does not change scripts: a script with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` keeps running under bash. Keep writing portable scripts in bash or sh, and use zsh for your terminal.
concepts.code:
zsh --version                 # zsh 5.9 (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu)
echo $SHELL                   # login shell from the user database, e.g. /bin/zsh
ps -p $$ -o comm=             # the shell you are actually in: zsh
echo $ZSH_VERSION             # 5.9  (empty in bash)
grep zsh /etc/shells          # /bin/zsh /usr/bin/zsh  (allowed for chsh)
chsh -s "$(command -v zsh)"   # make zsh your login shell; log in again
zsh -f                        # a clean zsh with no config files
./deploy.sh                   # a #!/usr/bin/env bash script still runs in bash
takeaways: Zsh is Bourne-compatible for everyday use and adds interactive features
$SHELL is the login shell; ps -p $$ shows the current shell
chsh -s changes the login shell; scripts follow their shebang
pitfalls: Assuming $SHELL tells you which shell is running right now.

quiz.q: You switched your terminal to zsh. Which shell runs a script whose first line is #!/usr/bin/env bash?
quiz.explain: The kernel uses the shebang interpreter, regardless of your interactive shell.

quiz.q: What is `zsh -f` useful for?
options: Running zsh faster by skipping completion only
Starting zsh without any startup files to test your config
quiz.explain: -f (NO_RCS) skips the startup files, so you can tell whether a problem comes from your configuration.

concepts.name: Startup files: .zshenv, .zprofile, .zshrc
concepts.summary: Which zsh config file is read when, and what belongs in each one.
concepts.why: Putting settings in the wrong file causes slow scripts, missing PATH entries and confusing behaviour.
concepts.body:
Zsh reads up to four user files, each after its system-wide twin in `/etc`, in this order:

- `~/.zshenv`: read by **every** zsh, including scripts and `zsh -c`. Keep it tiny and silent: a few environment variables at most.
- `~/.zprofile`: login shells, before `.zshrc`. A good place for `PATH` and other environment setup.
- `~/.zshrc`: **interactive** shells. Aliases, options, completion, key bindings and the prompt go here.
- `~/.zlogin`: login shells, after `.zshrc`; rarely needed. `~/.zlogout` runs when a login shell exits.

Unlike bash, an interactive login shell reads **both** `.zprofile` and `.zshrc`, so there is no need to source one from the other. On macOS every new Terminal tab is a login shell, while most Linux terminal emulators start non-login shells.

On macOS, `/etc/zprofile` runs `path_helper`, which reorders `PATH`; entries you add in `.zshenv` can end up behind system directories, which is another reason to set `PATH` in `.zprofile`.

`ZDOTDIR` relocates these files (for example to `~/.config/zsh`); set it in `~/.zshenv`. After editing, `exec zsh` replaces your shell with a fresh one, which is cleaner than `source ~/.zshrc` because settings removed from the file really disappear.
concepts.code:
# Order for an interactive login shell (e.g. a macOS Terminal tab):
#   /etc/zshenv  ~/.zshenv  ->  /etc/zprofile  ~/.zprofile
#   ->  /etc/zshrc  ~/.zshrc  ->  /etc/zlogin  ~/.zlogin
# ~/.zshenv   : every zsh, scripts included -> keep it tiny
export EDITOR=vim
# ~/.zprofile : login shells -> PATH and environment
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
# ~/.zshrc    : interactive shells -> aliases, options, prompt, completion
alias ll='ls -lah'
setopt AUTO_CD
# Reload after editing:
exec zsh
# See which files actually run at startup:
zsh -o SOURCE_TRACE -i -c exit 2>&1 | head
takeaways: .zshenv: every shell, keep minimal; .zprofile: login; .zshrc: interactive
Interactive login shells read both .zprofile and .zshrc
exec zsh reloads cleanly
pitfalls: Printing output or running slow commands in ~/.zshenv, which affects every script and scp session.

quiz.q: Where should aliases and the prompt be defined?
quiz.explain: .zshrc is read by interactive shells, which are the only ones that use aliases and prompts.

quiz.q: Which file is read even by a non-interactive `zsh script.zsh`?
quiz.explain: .zshenv is read by every zsh invocation unless -f or NO_RCS is used.

concepts.name: Tab completion
concepts.summary: Turn on zsh's completion system, get a navigable menu and complete options, branches, hosts and paths.
concepts.why: Completion is the single biggest productivity win of zsh, and it needs two lines to enable.
concepts.body:
Zsh's completion system (**compsys**) knows the options and arguments of hundreds of commands. It is enabled by loading and running `compinit`, which frameworks such as Oh My Zsh do for you. Once on:

- `git checkout <Tab>` offers branches, `ssh <Tab>` hosts from `~/.ssh/config`, `kill <Tab>` processes, `tar -<Tab>` options with descriptions,
- partial paths expand: `cd /u/lo/b<Tab>` becomes `cd /usr/local/bin/`,
- pressing Tab again cycles through candidates, and Ctrl-D lists them without inserting.

Behaviour is configured with **zstyle**, which sets a style for a context pattern. The two most popular: `zstyle ':completion:*' menu select` gives an arrow-key menu, and a `matcher-list` that makes matching case-insensitive. Styles are covered in depth when you write your own completions.

`compinit` caches what it finds in `~/.zcompdump`. If a newly installed tool has no completion, delete that file and start a new shell. compinit also checks that completion directories are not writable by other users and warns about "insecure directories"; `compaudit` lists them so you can fix their permissions instead of silencing the check.

Keep `compinit` after any changes to `fpath` (plugins add directories there), otherwise their completions are not found.
concepts.code:
# ~/.zshrc
autoload -Uz compinit && compinit        # turn on the completion system
zstyle ':completion:*' menu select       # arrow-key menu for candidates
zstyle ':completion:*' matcher-list 'm:{a-z}={A-Za-z}'   # case-insensitive
zstyle ':completion:*:descriptions' format '%B%d%b'      # bold group headings
# Then try, pressing Tab where marked:
#   cd /u/lo/b<Tab>      ->  cd /usr/local/bin/
#   git checkout ma<Tab> ->  matching branch names
#   tar -<Tab>           ->  every option with a description
#   kill <Tab>           ->  running processes with their PIDs
#   ssh <Tab>            ->  hosts from ~/.ssh/config and known_hosts
compaudit                                # lists insecure completion dirs, if any
rm -f ~/.zcompdump && exec zsh           # rebuild the completion cache
takeaways: autoload -Uz compinit && compinit enables completion
zstyle ':completion:*' menu select gives an interactive menu
Delete ~/.zcompdump when new completions do not show up
pitfalls: Calling compinit before plugins add their directories to fpath, so their completions are missing.

quiz.q: What does `zstyle ':completion:*' menu select` change?
options: Candidates can be chosen with the arrow keys
quiz.explain: menu select turns the candidate list into a navigable menu.

quiz.q: A tool you just installed has a completion file but Tab does nothing. A likely fix?
options: Delete ~/.zcompdump and start a new shell
quiz.explain: compinit caches discovered completions in ~/.zcompdump; rebuilding it picks up new ones.

concepts.name: Recursive globs and qualifiers
concepts.summary: Use ** for recursive matching and glob qualifiers like (.), (/) and (om) to filter and sort files.
concepts.why: Zsh globs replace most simple find commands with something shorter you can type at the prompt.
concepts.body:
Zsh supports the same `*`, `?` and `[...]` patterns as bash, plus a few things that make it shine at the prompt.

**Recursive globbing** is always on: `**/*.py` matches Python files in this directory and every subdirectory (bash needs `shopt -s globstar`).

**Glob qualifiers** go in parentheses at the end of a pattern and filter or sort the matches:

- `(.)` regular files, `(/)` directories, `(@)` symlinks, `(*)` executables,
- `(om)` sort by modification time, newest first; `(on)` by name,
- `[1]` or `[1,3]` take the first match or a range: `*(om[1])` is the newest file,
- `(N)` makes this pattern expand to nothing if it matches nothing.

The biggest difference from bash: when a pattern matches nothing, zsh reports **"no matches found"** and does not run the command (option `NOMATCH`). Bash would pass the literal pattern along. This bites with URLs and arguments containing `?`, `*` or `[`, such as `curl https://x.io/?q=1` or `pip install foo[dev]`: quote them, or prefix the command with `noglob`.

Use `print -l` (one item per line) to preview what a glob expands to before using it with `rm` or `mv`.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
mkdir -p src/lib && touch src/a.py src/lib/b.py notes.txt
print -l **/*.py        # src/a.py  src/lib/b.py   (recursive, built in)
print -l *(/)           # src         (directories only)
print -l **/*(.)        # every regular file, recursively
touch -d '2 days ago' old.txt
print -l *.txt(om)      # notes.txt old.txt   (newest first)
print -l *.txt(om[1])   # notes.txt           (just the newest)
print -l *.zip(N)       # (nothing: N = null glob for this pattern)
print 'https://x.io/?q=1'   # quote URLs: ? is a glob character
ls *.zip                # zsh: no matches found: *.zip
takeaways: ** is recursive by default
Qualifiers like (.) (/) (om[1]) filter and sort matches
No match is an error in zsh; quote URLs or use (N) / noglob
pitfalls: Running `pip install requests[socks]` unquoted and getting 'no matches found'.

quiz.q: Which glob expands to the most recently modified file in the directory?
quiz.explain: om sorts by modification time, newest first, and [1] picks the first match.

quiz.q: `curl https://api.example.com/items?id=4` fails with 'no matches found'. Why?
options: The ? is treated as a glob that matches no file
quiz.explain: Unquoted ? is a glob character; zsh refuses to run a command with an unmatched pattern.

concepts.name: Options and shared history
concepts.summary: Turn zsh behaviour on and off with setopt, and configure a large, shared, de-duplicated history.
concepts.why: A handful of options and history settings make the shell noticeably nicer to live in.
concepts.body:
Most zsh behaviour is controlled by named **options**. `setopt NAME` turns one on, `unsetopt NAME` (or `setopt NO_NAME`) turns it off. Names are case-insensitive and underscores are ignored, so `AUTO_CD`, `autocd` and `AutoCd` are the same option. Plain `setopt` lists the options that differ from their defaults, and `[[ -o name ]]` tests one.

Popular interactive options:

- `AUTO_CD`: type a directory name alone to cd into it,
- `AUTO_PUSHD` and `PUSHD_IGNORE_DUPS`: every cd pushes onto a stack; `cd -<Tab>` and `dirs -v` let you jump back,
- `INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS`: allow `#` comments at the prompt (off by default!),
- `CORRECT`: offer to fix mistyped commands.

**History** is not saved unless you configure it. Set `HISTFILE` to a path, `HISTSIZE` (entries kept in memory) and `SAVEHIST` (entries written to the file). Then add:

- `SHARE_HISTORY`: all open shells read and append to the same history as you go,
- `HIST_IGNORE_ALL_DUPS`: drop older duplicates,
- `HIST_IGNORE_SPACE`: commands typed with a leading space are not recorded, useful for secrets,
- `EXTENDED_HISTORY`: store timestamps and durations.

`history` (an alias of `fc -l`) shows entries; `history -i` adds ISO timestamps, and `!!`, `!$` and `!git` history expansion work as in bash.
concepts.code:
# ~/.zshrc
setopt AUTO_CD                        # 'projects' alone -> cd projects
setopt AUTO_PUSHD PUSHD_IGNORE_DUPS   # cd builds a stack: cd -<Tab>, dirs -v
setopt INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS           # allow # comments at the prompt
setopt CORRECT                        # zsh: correct 'gti' to 'git' [nyae]?
HISTFILE=~/.zsh_history
HISTSIZE=50000                        # entries kept in memory
SAVEHIST=50000                        # entries written to HISTFILE
setopt SHARE_HISTORY                  # all shells share one live history
setopt HIST_IGNORE_ALL_DUPS HIST_IGNORE_SPACE EXTENDED_HISTORY
# At the prompt:
setopt                                # options that differ from defaults
[[ -o autocd ]] && echo "autocd on"   # case and underscores do not matter
history -i -5                         # last 5 entries with timestamps
takeaways: setopt / unsetopt; names ignore case and underscores
History is only saved with HISTFILE and SAVEHIST set
SHARE_HISTORY and HIST_IGNORE_SPACE are the favourite history options
pitfalls: Expecting history to persist without setting HISTFILE and SAVEHIST.

quiz.q: Which pair of settings is needed for zsh to write history to disk?
quiz.explain: HISTFILE names the file and SAVEHIST says how many entries to write to it.

quiz.q: Are `setopt AUTO_CD` and `setopt autocd` the same?
options: Yes: option names ignore case and underscores
No, only the upper-case form works
No, autocd is a different option
quiz.explain: Zsh normalises option names by ignoring case and underscores.

concepts.name: Customizing the prompt
concepts.summary: Build a prompt with % escapes, colours, exit-status conditionals and the git branch via vcs_info.
concepts.why: A good prompt shows where you are, which branch you are on and whether the last command failed.
concepts.body:
The prompt is the `PROMPT` variable (alias `PS1`); `RPROMPT` is shown on the right and disappears as you type into it. Zsh expands **percent escapes** in them:

- `%n` user, `%m` short host name, `%~` current directory with `~` for home, `%1~` only its last component,
- `%#` shows `#` for root and `%` otherwise, `%?` the last exit status, `%T` the time,
- `%F{red}...%f` foreground colour (names or 0-255), `%B...%b` bold,
- `%(?.yes.no)` a conditional: here "yes" if the last command succeeded.

To include the output of variables or functions that change, set `PROMPT_SUBST` and write the prompt in **single quotes**, so `${...}` is expanded every time the prompt is drawn rather than once when `.zshrc` runs.

For the git branch, zsh ships **vcs_info**: load it, call `vcs_info` from the `precmd` hook (run before each prompt), and use `$vcs_info_msg_0_`. Its `formats` style uses `%b` for the branch; it can also show staged or unstaged changes.

`print -P '...'` expands prompt escapes so you can experiment. If you prefer a ready-made prompt, Powerlevel10k and the cross-shell Starship are popular, but understanding the escapes lets you read and tweak them.
concepts.code:
autoload -Uz vcs_info
precmd() { vcs_info }                       # refresh before each prompt
zstyle ':vcs_info:git:*' formats ' (%b)'    # %b = branch name
setopt PROMPT_SUBST
PROMPT='%F{cyan}%n@%m%f %F{yellow}%~%f${vcs_info_msg_0_} %(?.%F{green}.%F{red})%#%f '
RPROMPT='%F{240}%T%f'                       # time on the right
print -P '%F{yellow}%~%f'                   # try escapes: ~/projects/app
print -P 'last: %(?.ok.failed with %?)'     # last: ok
# The result looks like:
# ada@laptop ~/projects/app (main) %                     12:41
takeaways: %n %m %~ %# %? are the core prompt escapes
%F{color}...%f for colour, %(?.ok.fail) for conditionals
PROMPT_SUBST plus single quotes for values that change, vcs_info for git
pitfalls: Writing PROMPT in double quotes with ${...}, so the value is frozen when .zshrc runs.

quiz.q: What does %(?.✔.✘) show after a failing command?
quiz.explain: %(?.a.b) shows a when the last exit status was 0 and b otherwise.

quiz.q: Why is the prompt written in single quotes with PROMPT_SUBST set?
options: So ${...} is expanded each time the prompt is drawn
Double quotes are invalid in PROMPT
quiz.explain: Single quotes keep ${...} literal in the variable; PROMPT_SUBST expands it on every redraw.

concepts.name: Plugins, frameworks and aliases
concepts.summary: Add autosuggestions and syntax highlighting, choose between a framework and plain sourcing, and use global and suffix aliases.
concepts.why: Plugins give fish-like suggestions and highlighting, but each one costs startup time.
concepts.body:
A zsh **plugin** is just a script you `source` from `.zshrc`, sometimes adding a directory to `fpath` for completions. Two are near-universal:

- **zsh-autosuggestions**: shows a grey suggestion from history as you type; Right arrow or End accepts it.
- **zsh-syntax-highlighting**: colours the command line, red for unknown commands. Source it **last**, after other plugins and key bindings.

You can manage plugins three ways: clone repositories and source them yourself, use a lightweight plugin manager (antidote, zinit, zap), or use a framework. **Oh My Zsh** is the best-known framework: it bundles hundreds of plugins (`plugins=(git docker kubectl)`) and themes. It is convenient but loads a lot; measure with `time zsh -i -c exit` and keep the list short.

Beyond normal aliases, zsh has two extra kinds:

- **global aliases** (`alias -g G='| grep -i'`) expand anywhere on the line, not only in command position,
- **suffix aliases** (`alias -s md=less`) open a file by typing its name: `README.md` runs `less README.md`.

Use global aliases sparingly: they expand even inside arguments where you did not expect them. `alias` with no arguments lists everything currently defined, which helps when a framework surprises you.
concepts.code:
# Manual setup (no framework): clone once, then source in ~/.zshrc
git clone https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-autosuggestions ~/.zsh/zsh-autosuggestions
git clone https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-syntax-highlighting ~/.zsh/zsh-syntax-highlighting
# ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zsh/zsh-autosuggestions/zsh-autosuggestions.zsh
alias gs='git status'          # normal alias: command position only
alias -g G='| grep -i'         # global alias: anywhere in the line
alias -s md=less               # suffix alias: README.md -> less README.md
source ~/.zsh/zsh-syntax-highlighting/zsh-syntax-highlighting.zsh   # last
# At the prompt:
ps aux G zsh                   # runs: ps aux | grep -i zsh
time zsh -i -c exit            # how long your config takes to load
# With Oh My Zsh instead, in ~/.zshrc:  plugins=(git docker kubectl)
takeaways: Plugins are sourced scripts; source syntax highlighting last
alias -g expands anywhere, alias -s opens files by extension
Measure startup time and keep plugins few
pitfalls: Loading dozens of Oh My Zsh plugins and then living with a one-second shell startup.

quiz.q: After `alias -g L='| less'`, what does `cat log.txt L` run?
quiz.explain: Global aliases are expanded anywhere on the command line.

quiz.q: Why should zsh-syntax-highlighting be sourced last?
options: It needs to wrap widgets that other plugins and bindings define
It must run after compinit only
quiz.explain: It hooks the line editor's widgets, so widgets created later would not be highlighted.

concepts.name: Scripting differences from bash
concepts.summary: No word splitting, 1-based arrays, typeset -A, last pipe stage in the current shell, and emulate for compatibility.
concepts.why: Pasting bash snippets into zsh (or the reverse) breaks in subtle ways unless you know these differences.
concepts.body:
Zsh scripts look like bash scripts, but several defaults differ:

- **No word splitting of unquoted variables.** With `v="a b"`, `$v` stays one word. Use `${=v}` to split explicitly, or `setopt SH_WORD_SPLIT`. Globs inside variable values are not expanded either unless you write `${~v}`.
- **Arrays are 1-based**: `$arr[1]` is the first element, `$arr[-1]` the last, `$#arr` the length, `$arr[2,3]` a slice. `$arr` alone gives all elements, and empty elements are dropped unless you use `"${arr[@]}"`.
- **Associative arrays**: `typeset -A m`; `${(k)m}` lists keys, `${(v)m}` values.
- `read -A` (not `-a`) reads words into an array.
- The **last stage of a pipeline runs in the current shell**, so `cmd | read v` sets `v`.
- An unmatched glob is an error (`NOMATCH`); use `(N)`.

Prefer `print` over `echo` (`print -r --` for raw output, `print -l` one argument per line); like zsh's `echo`, plain `print` interprets backslash escapes.

For code that must behave like sh or ksh, `emulate -L sh` inside a function switches to those rules for that function only (`-L` makes options local). Conversely, libraries meant to work under any user configuration start with `emulate -L zsh` to get default zsh options.
concepts.code:
words="one two three"
for w in $words; do print -- "<$w>"; done              # <one two three>
for w in ${=words}; do print -n -- "<$w>"; done; print # <one><two><three>
arr=(alpha beta gamma)
print $arr[1] $arr[-1] $#arr          # alpha gamma 3   (1-based)
print $arr[2,3]                       # beta gamma
typeset -A port=(http 80 https 443)
print $port[https]                    # 443
print ${(k)port}                      # https http  (order not guaranteed)
echo hi | read v; print "v=$v"        # v=hi   (in bash: v=)
read -A parts <<< "x y z"; print $#parts   # 3
f() { emulate -L sh; s="a b"; set -- $s; print $#; }
f                                     # 2   (sh rules: word splitting on)
print -l -- *.nomatch(N) done         # done
takeaways: Unquoted $var is not split in zsh; ${=var} splits explicitly
Arrays start at 1; $#arr is the length
emulate -L sh or zsh sets predictable rules inside a function
pitfalls: Porting a bash loop over `$list` and getting a single iteration because zsh does not split it.

quiz.q: In zsh, with arr=(a b c), what is $arr[1]?
quiz.explain: Zsh arrays are 1-based unless KSH_ARRAYS is set.

quiz.q: In zsh, `v="x y"; for i in $v; do print $i; done` prints how many lines?
quiz.explain: Zsh does not word-split unquoted parameter expansions by default.

concepts.name: Qualifiers, modifiers and extended globs
concepts.summary: Filter files by size, age and owner, transform paths with :t :h :r :e and use ^ and ~ with EXTENDED_GLOB.
concepts.why: These replace find, basename and dirname in one-liners, and work on variables too.
concepts.body:
Glob qualifiers combine freely inside one pair of parentheses:

- **size** `L`: `(Lk+100)` larger than 100 KB, `(Lm-1)` smaller than 1 MB,
- **time** `m` (modified), `a` (accessed), `c` (changed): `(mh-1)` within the last hour, `(md+30)` more than 30 days ago,
- **owner**: `(U)` owned by you, `(u:root:)` by root; `(D)` includes dotfiles,
- **sorting** with `o` (ascending) or `O` (descending) followed by `n` name, `L` size, `m` mtime; then a subscript like `[1,5]`,
- `^` negates the next qualifier, `,` means OR between groups, and `(e:'expr':)` or `(+func)` run arbitrary tests.

**Modifiers** transform each match and also work on variables: `:t` tail (basename), `:h` head (dirname), `:r` root (drop the extension), `:e` extension, `:a` absolute path, `:u` and `:l` change case. `$f:t` or `${f:r}` work on any variable.

With `setopt EXTENDED_GLOB` you get pattern operators: `^*.log` everything not matching, `pat~exclude` match then exclude, `#` and `##` for repetition, and `(#i)` for case-insensitive matching.

Zsh also has short loop forms (`for f in *.txt; mv ...` without do/done), which are handy at the prompt; use full syntax in scripts. For renaming many files, the bundled `zmv` function (`autoload -Uz zmv`) is safer than a loop.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
mkdir logs && print x > a.txt && head -c 200000 /dev/zero > big.bin
touch -d '40 days ago' logs/old.log && touch logs/new.log
print -l **/*(.Lk+100)          # big.bin         (larger than 100 KB)
print -l **/*.log(.md+30)       # logs/old.log    (modified > 30 days ago)
print -l *(.oL)                 # a.txt big.bin   (by size, smallest first)
f=/srv/app/report.final.csv
print $f:t $f:h                 # report.final.csv /srv/app
print $f:r $f:e                 # /srv/app/report.final csv
print -l logs/*(.:t:r)          # new old   (modifiers inside qualifiers)
setopt EXTENDED_GLOB
print -l *~*.bin                # a.txt logs    (~ excludes)
print -l **/^*.log(.)           # a.txt big.bin (^ negates the pattern)
for f in *.txt; mv -- $f $f:r.md      # short loop form: rename .txt -> .md
print -l *(.)                   # a.md big.bin
takeaways: L size, m/a/c time, U/u owner, o/O sort, [n,m] range
:t :h :r :e modifiers work on matches and on variables
EXTENDED_GLOB adds ^ negation and ~ exclusion
pitfalls: Forgetting the (.) qualifier, so directories are included in a destructive command.

quiz.q: Which glob lists regular files larger than 1 MB, recursively?
quiz.explain: (.) restricts to regular files and Lm+1 means larger than 1 MB; mh is a time qualifier.

quiz.q: With f=photos/cat.jpeg, what does $f:r give?
quiz.explain: :r removes the extension but keeps the directory part; :t:r would give cat.

concepts.name: The line editor (ZLE) and custom widgets
concepts.summary: Configure key bindings with bindkey, use prefix history search and write your own ZLE widgets.
concepts.why: ZLE is what makes zsh's command line programmable: any editing action can be bound to any key.
concepts.body:
Everything you type at the prompt goes through **ZLE**, the Zsh Line Editor. Every action, from moving the cursor to searching history, is a **widget**, and **keymaps** bind key sequences to widgets.

- `bindkey -e` selects emacs-style keys (the default unless your `EDITOR` contains "vi"); `bindkey -v` selects vi mode.
- `bindkey` alone lists all bindings; `bindkey '^R'` shows one. `zle -al` lists all widgets.
- Press Ctrl-V and then a key to see the sequence it sends, such as `^[[A` for Up in most terminals.

Useful bundled widgets: `up-line-or-beginning-search` makes Up search history for lines starting with what you already typed; `edit-command-line` opens the current line in `$EDITOR`. Bundled widget functions must be loaded with `autoload -Uz name` and registered with `zle -N name` before binding.

A **custom widget** is a shell function registered with `zle -N`. Inside it you can read and change special variables: `BUFFER` (the whole line), `LBUFFER` and `RBUFFER` (text left and right of the cursor) and `CURSOR` (position). `zle -M "text"` shows a message under the prompt, and calling `zle accept-line` runs the line. Key bindings and widgets belong in `.zshrc`, and should be set before plugins like syntax highlighting that wrap existing widgets.
concepts.code:
bindkey -e                                  # emacs keys (-v for vi mode)
autoload -Uz up-line-or-beginning-search down-line-or-beginning-search
zle -N up-line-or-beginning-search
zle -N down-line-or-beginning-search
bindkey '^[[A' up-line-or-beginning-search  # Up: history matching the typed prefix
bindkey '^[[B' down-line-or-beginning-search
autoload -Uz edit-command-line && zle -N edit-command-line
bindkey '^X^E' edit-command-line            # edit the line in $EDITOR
# A custom widget: Alt-s puts sudo in front of the current line
prepend-sudo() {
  [[ $BUFFER == sudo\ * ]] || BUFFER="sudo $BUFFER"
  CURSOR=$#BUFFER                           # cursor to the end
  zle -M "sudo added"
}
zle -N prepend-sudo
bindkey '^[s' prepend-sudo
bindkey '^R'                                # "^R" history-incremental-search-backward
takeaways: Widgets are actions; bindkey maps key sequences to them
Custom widget = function + zle -N + bindkey
BUFFER, LBUFFER, RBUFFER and CURSOR expose the command line
pitfalls: Binding a bundled widget like edit-command-line without autoload and zle -N, which gives 'No such widget'.

quiz.q: What are the three steps to bind your own function `myw` to Ctrl-G?
options: define myw; zle -N myw; bindkey '^G' myw
quiz.explain: The function must be registered as a widget with zle -N before it can be bound.

quiz.q: Inside a widget, which variable holds the text to the left of the cursor?
quiz.explain: LBUFFER is everything before the cursor, RBUFFER everything after.

concepts.name: Parameter expansion flags
concepts.summary: Split, join, sort, deduplicate, change case and search arrays with ${(flags)name} and subscript flags.
concepts.why: Flags let zsh do in one expansion what bash needs loops or external tools for.
concepts.body:
Zsh puts **flags** in parentheses right after the opening brace: `${(flags)name}`. Several can be combined and expansions nest, with the inner result feeding the outer one.

- **Split and join**: `(s:,:)` splits on a string, `(f)` splits on newlines (the most common way to turn command output into an array), `(j:,:)` joins with a separator, `(F)` joins with newlines.
- **Case**: `(U)` upper, `(L)` lower, `(C)` capitalise words.
- **Order and uniqueness**: `(o)` sort ascending, `(O)` descending, `(n)` numeric sort, `(u)` unique.
- **Associative arrays**: `(k)` keys, `(v)` values, `(kv)` pairs.
- **Quoting**: `(q)` quotes the value for safe reuse as shell input, `(Q)` removes one level of quoting.
- **Indirection**: `(P)` treats the value as the name of another parameter.
- `(@)` keeps array elements separate inside double quotes, like `"${arr[@]}"`.

**Subscript flags** search arrays: `$arr[(i)value]` gives the index of the first match (one past the end if missing), `$arr[(r)pattern]` the first matching element, `(I)` and `(R)` search from the end.

**Nesting** avoids temporaries: `${${f:t}%%.*}` takes the base name, then strips every extension. `${:-text}` creates a value from literal text, handy as the innermost expansion. Splitting with `(s)` drops empty fields unless the expansion is quoted with `(@)`.
concepts.code:
csv="b,a,c,a"
parts=(${(s:,:)csv})
print $#parts                       # 4
print ${(j:-:)parts}                # b-a-c-a
print ${(uo)parts}                  # a b c   (unique, sorted)
print ${(U)csv}                     # B,A,C,A
lines=(${(f)"$(printf 'x 1\ny 2\n')"})
print $#lines                       # 2   (split on newlines)
fruits=(apple banana cherry)
print $fruits[(i)banana]            # 2   (index of the element)
print $fruits[(i)kiwi]              # 4   (not found: length + 1)
print $fruits[(r)c*]                # cherry
ref=fruits
print ${(P)ref}                     # apple banana cherry  (indirection)
f=/a/b/archive.tar.gz
print ${${f:t}%%.*}                 # archive  (nested expansion)
s="it's here"
print -r -- ${(q)s}                 # it\'s\ here
takeaways: ${(s:x:)v} splits, ${(j:x:)arr} joins, (f) splits lines
(o) (O) (u) sort and deduplicate; (k) (v) for maps
$arr[(i)x] and $arr[(r)pat] search arrays
pitfalls: Using plain print to show (q) output: print interprets the backslashes again; use print -r.

quiz.q: What does ${(j:,:)${(s: :)${:-c a b}}} produce?
quiz.explain: The literal is split on spaces into (c a b) and joined with commas; no sorting flag is used.

quiz.q: With arr=(x y z), what is $arr[(i)q]?
quiz.explain: The (i) subscript returns one past the last index when nothing matches.

concepts.name: Writing completions with compsys
concepts.summary: Write a _command completion function with _arguments and _describe, register it via fpath and tune it with zstyle.
concepts.why: Completions for your own tools and scripts make them as pleasant to use as git or docker.
concepts.body:
A completion is a function named after the command with a leading underscore, `_deploy`, stored in a file of the same name in a directory on **fpath**. The file's first line `#compdef deploy` tells `compinit` which commands it completes. compinit scans fpath when it builds `~/.zcompdump`, so add your directory to fpath **before** calling compinit.

Most completions are built on `_arguments`, which takes one spec per option or argument:

- `'-v[verbose output]'` an option with a description,
- `'(-v --verbose)'{-v,--verbose}'[...]'` both spellings, excluding each other,
- `'--config=[config file]:file:_files'` an option with a value and an action that completes it,
- `'1:environment:->env'` the first positional argument, handled in a `case $state` block,
- `'*:service:(api web worker)'` any further arguments from a fixed list.

`_describe` offers values with descriptions (`'staging:test environment'`), and helpers like `_files`, `_hosts` and `_users` complete common things. For a tool whose `--help` lists its options, `compdef _gnu_generic mytool` gives decent completion for free.

Styles use the context `:completion:function:completer:command:argument:tag`, for example `zstyle ':completion:*:*:deploy:*' ...`. Press Ctrl-X then `?` to run `_complete_debug`, which writes a trace of the completion to a file. After changing completion files, remove `~/.zcompdump` and start a new shell.
concepts.code:
#compdef deploy
# file: ~/.zsh/completions/_deploy
local state
local -a envs=('staging:test environment' 'production:live site')
_arguments -s \
  '(-v --verbose)'{-v,--verbose}'[print more output]' \
  '(-t --tag)'{-t+,--tag=}'[image tag to deploy]:tag:' \
  '--config=[config file]:file:_files -g "*.(yml|yaml)"' \
  '1:environment:->env' \
  '*:service:(api web worker)'
case $state in
  env) _describe -t envs 'environment' envs ;;
esac
# In ~/.zshrc, BEFORE compinit:
#   fpath=(~/.zsh/completions $fpath)
#   autoload -Uz compinit && compinit
#   compdef _gnu_generic mytool    # free completion from mytool --help
# deploy <Tab>     ->  production -- live site / staging -- test environment
# deploy -<Tab>    ->  --config --tag --verbose -t -v
takeaways: A _cmd file with #compdef cmd on fpath, loaded by compinit
_arguments specs describe options, values and positional arguments
->state plus case $state for custom logic; _describe for described values
pitfalls: Adding the completions directory to fpath after compinit has already run.

quiz.q: What does the first line `#compdef deploy` in a completion file do?
options: Tells compinit this function completes the deploy command
quiz.explain: compinit reads #compdef lines to map commands to completion functions.

quiz.q: In an _arguments spec, what does '*:file:_files' describe?
options: Any number of further arguments completed as files
quiz.explain: A leading * means the spec applies to all remaining positional arguments.

concepts.name: Autoloaded functions and startup speed
concepts.summary: Organise functions with fpath and autoload, profile startup with zprof and speed it up with caching and lazy loading.
concepts.why: A shell that opens instantly is the result of knowing where your startup time goes.
concepts.body:
**Autoloading** keeps `.zshrc` small. Put each function in its own file named after it, in a directory on `fpath`, and declare it with `autoload -Uz name`. The file holds only the function body. Nothing is read until the first call. `-U` disables alias expansion while loading (so your aliases cannot break it) and `-z` selects zsh-style loading. Most of zsh's bundled features (compinit, vcs_info, zmv) are autoloaded functions.

`typeset -U path` keeps the `path` array, which is **tied** to `PATH`, free of duplicates; edit `path=(dir $path)` like any array. The same works for `fpath`.

To find slow startup, put `zmodload zsh/zprof` at the very top of `.zshrc` and `zprof` at the bottom; it prints which functions took the most time. `time zsh -i -c exit` measures the total. Usual suspects:

- `compinit` checking and rebuilding the dump every time: call `compinit -C` when the dump is recent,
- version-manager init scripts (nvm, pyenv, conda): **lazy-load** them with a stub function that replaces itself on first use,
- frameworks loading many plugins, and commands like `brew --prefix` run on each start.

`zcompile` compiles scripts and function directories into `.zwc` wordcode files that load faster; zsh uses them automatically when they are newer than the source.
concepts.code:
# ~/.zshrc, first line:
zmodload zsh/zprof                    # start profiling
typeset -U path fpath                 # no duplicate entries
path=(~/.local/bin $path)             # tied to $PATH
fpath=(~/.zsh/functions $fpath)
autoload -Uz mkcd                     # body lives in ~/.zsh/functions/mkcd:
#   mkdir -p -- "$1" && cd -- "$1"
nvm() { unfunction nvm; source ~/.nvm/nvm.sh; nvm "$@"; }   # lazy-load
autoload -Uz compinit
setopt EXTENDED_GLOB
if [[ -n ~/.zcompdump(#qN.mh+24) ]]; then
  compinit                            # dump older than 24 h: full check
else
  compinit -C                         # recent dump: skip the check
fi
zcompile ~/.zshrc                     # writes ~/.zshrc.zwc
# last line:
zprof | head -n 15                    # functions sorted by time spent
takeaways: autoload -Uz name loads ~/fpath/name on first call
zmodload zsh/zprof + zprof finds slow startup code
Lazy-load heavy tools and use compinit -C with a fresh dump
pitfalls: Running `eval "$(slow-tool init)"` for several tools on every startup instead of lazy-loading.

quiz.q: What does `autoload -Uz mkcd` do immediately?
options: Reads and parses the mkcd file
Marks mkcd to be loaded from fpath on first use
quiz.explain: Autoload only registers the name; the file is read when the function is first called.

quiz.q: How do you see which parts of .zshrc are slow?
options: zmodload zsh/zprof at the top, zprof at the bottom
quiz.explain: zprof reports time spent per function since the module was loaded.
